Peru Lifts Nationwide Curfew as Power Plants, Businesses Resume Activity

LIMA, June 15 — Peru lifted its month-long nationwide curfew on Thursday, allowing factories, offices, and public services to resume normal operations and marking a significant step toward economic recovery after a surge in respiratory illness cases triggered sweeping health measures.

The curfew, imposed on May 12, restricted movement from 8 p.m. to 5 a.m. across all regions and forced the temporary closure of schools, markets, and many non-essential businesses. The government said the measure was necessary to contain the spread of an aggressive influenza outbreak that overwhelmed hospitals in Lima, Arequipa, and other major cities.

Power producers, including Enel Generacion Peru SAA, were among the companies affected by the shutdowns. The National Association of Electricity Companies (AEPE) reported that electricity demand fell by nearly 18% during the curfew period due to reduced industrial and commercial activity.

“With the improvement in public health indicators and the availability of vaccines, we are able to lift the curfew,” Health Minister Rosa Gamarra said at a press conference on Thursday. “We thank the public and business community for their cooperation in overcoming this emergency.”

Enel Generacion Peru SAA said in a statement that it had fully restored operations at its hydroelectric and thermal plants after conducting safety reviews. “We are committed to supporting the country’s recovery by ensuring a stable supply of electricity,” the company said.

Analysts said the curfew’s economic impact was broad, with the National Chamber of Commerce estimating losses of over $1.2 billion in retail, transport, and manufacturing. “The shutdown disrupted supply chains, especially for small and medium-sized enterprises,” said Javier Salinas, an economist at Universidad del Pacifico. “But quick action by authorities helped prevent a more severe public health crisis.”

Most shops and restaurants reopened early Friday, with workers returning under new hygiene protocols. Schools are scheduled to resume in-person classes next week. The Ministry of Health reported a steep decline in new influenza cases over the past 10 days, crediting both the movement restrictions and a nationwide vaccination campaign.

Union leaders welcomed the end of the curfew but urged continued support for affected workers. “Many families lost income during the closures,” said Maria Torres of the National Workers Federation. “We hope for measures to aid those still struggling as the economy rebounds.”

Officials said they would monitor infection rates closely and stood ready to reinstate targeted measures if needed.
